title: Building reusable automation modules with error handling
monthTitle: Automation: PowerShell & Microsoft Graph at Scale
summary: Package your scripts into a proper PowerShell module with a manifest, controlled exports, robust error handling, structured logging, and Pester tests.
objectives: Structure a script module (.psm1) and manifest (.psd1) the right way
Control which functions are public versus internal with Export-ModuleMember
Build robust error handling with try/catch/finally and custom error records
Add structured logging and verbose output that callers can toggle
Add retry with exponential backoff as a reusable helper
Write a basic Pester test to protect a function's behaviour

quiz.q: What is the role of the module manifest (.psd1)?
options: It declares metadata, version, dependencies, and what the module exports
It is optional and ignored by PowerShell
quiz.why: The .psd1 manifest declares the module's version, author, required modules, and the functions/cmdlets it exports, while the .psm1 holds the actual code.

quiz.q: How do you keep a helper function internal to a module so callers cannot use it directly?
options: Name it with a lowercase letter
Do not list it in FunctionsToExport / Export-ModuleMember
quiz.why: Only functions you explicitly export (via Export-ModuleMember or FunctionsToExport in the manifest) are public; everything else stays private to the module scope.

quiz.q: What is the advantage of throwing a custom error record with a meaningful category and target?
options: Callers can catch specific error types and get actionable context for diagnostics
quiz.why: A well-formed ErrorRecord (message, category, target object) lets callers branch on the failure type and gives operators the context they need, rather than a generic opaque failure.

quiz.q: In a retry-with-backoff helper, why increase the wait time after each failed attempt?
options: To make the script slower on purpose
To avoid hammering a struggling or throttling service and give it time to recover
quiz.why: Exponential backoff spaces out retries so you stop pounding a service that is rate-limiting or temporarily down, which is both more polite and more likely to succeed.

quiz.q: Name the testing framework you would use to write automated tests for your PowerShell module.
quiz.answer: Pester — the de facto PowerShell testing framework, using Describe/It blocks and Should assertions to test functions and mock dependencies.
quiz.why: Pester lets you assert behaviour and mock Graph calls so you can test logic without touching a live tenant, which is essential for reliable, refactorable modules.

quiz.q: In one sentence, why prefer Write-Verbose and a logging function over Write-Host inside a module?
quiz.answer: Write-Host writes straight to the host and cannot be captured or toggled, whereas Write-Verbose and a logging function let callers control detail and redirect or persist logs.
quiz.why: Modules are consumed by other scripts and runbooks, so output must be controllable and capturable rather than hard-printed to a screen that may not exist.

slides.title: Building reusable automation modules with error handling
slides.sub: Month 2 - Automation: PowerShell & Microsoft Graph at Scale  |  Lesson 6
slides.narration: You now have a growing pile of useful functions. This lesson is about turning that pile into a proper, reusable PowerShell module: a manifest, controlled exports, real error handling, logging, retries, and tests. This is the difference between scripts that live on one technician's laptop and automation the whole team can depend on.

slides.title: From scripts to a module
bullets: A module packages related functions.
Others Import-Module and call your work.
Two files: .psm1 code, .psd1 manifest.
The manifest declares version and exports.
slides.code:
EndpointOps/
  EndpointOps.psd1   # manifest
  EndpointOps.psm1   # code + Export-ModuleMember
slides.narration: Once you have more than a handful of functions, copy pasting them between scripts becomes a liability. A PowerShell module packages related functions so others can Import dash Module them and call your work like built in cmdlets. A script module is two files: a dot p s m one holding the code, and a dot p s d one, the manifest, that declares metadata, version, dependencies, and what the module exports. Folder name, module name, and root module should all line up.

slides.title: Generate the manifest
bullets: Use New-ModuleManifest, never hand-write the GUID.
Set ModuleVersion and bump it on changes.
Declare RequiredModules so dependencies install.
List FunctionsToExport explicitly.
slides.narration: Generate the manifest with New dash Module Manifest, and never hand edit the auto generated G U I D. Set a Module Version and bump it whenever you change the module, because version numbers are how runbooks and other scripts pin to a known good build. Declare Required Modules so your dependencies, like Microsoft dot Graph dot Authentication, install automatically. And list Functions To Export explicitly, which leads us to the next point: deciding what is public.

slides.title: Public vs internal functions
bullets: Only exported functions are callable from outside.
Unexported functions are private helpers.
Control with FunctionsToExport or Export-ModuleMember.
Keep your public surface small and intentional.
slides.code:
Export-ModuleMember -Function 'Get-StaleDevice','Invoke-DeviceSyncBulk'
# Write-Log and Invoke-WithRetry stay internal
slides.narration: Not everything should be callable from outside your module. Only the functions you export are public. Everything else stays private to the module scope and acts as an internal helper. You control this with Functions To Export in the manifest or Export dash Module Member in the p s m one. Keep your public surface small and intentional, because every public function is a promise you have to keep stable. Helpers like Write dash Log and Invoke dash With Retry stay internal.

slides.title: Error handling that helps
bullets: Generic failures waste hours.
Throw meaningful error records with category and target.
Use try/catch/finally; re-throw with detail.
Never silently swallow errors.
slides.narration: Generic, opaque failures waste hours of someone's life. Throw meaningful error records that carry a category and a target object, so callers can catch a specific type and operators get real context. Use try catch finally, and when you catch an error, re throw it with added detail rather than swallowing it. A caught error you ignore is a future incident. Here we surface which device failed and why, with an Object Not Found category that a caller can branch on.

slides.title: Reusable logging
bullets: Give the module an internal Write-Log helper.
Timestamp and level every message.
Route through Write-Verbose, not Write-Host.
Callers can toggle and capture the detail.
slides.narration: Give your module one internal logging function that every public function uses. Timestamp and level each message, and route it through Write dash Verbose rather than Write dash Host. Why? Because a module is consumed by other scripts and runbooks where there may be no screen at all. Write dash Host writes straight to a host and cannot be captured or toggled, but Write dash Verbose lets callers switch detail on with dash Verbose and redirect or persist the log. Controllable output is the whole point.

slides.title: Retry with exponential backoff
bullets: Wrap flaky calls in a retry helper.
Increase the wait after each failed attempt.
Backoff avoids hammering a throttling service.
Re-throw on the final attempt.
slides.narration: Network and Graph calls fail intermittently, so give your module a retry with backoff helper. It runs an action, and if it throws, it waits and tries again, increasing the delay after each failure: two seconds, then four, then eight. That exponential backoff stops you hammering a service that is throttling or temporarily down, giving it room to recover. On the final attempt it re throws so a genuine failure still surfaces. Now any public function can wrap a flaky Graph call in Invoke dash With Retry and get resilience for free.

slides.title: Test with Pester
bullets: A module you cannot test you cannot safely change.
Pester uses Describe and It blocks.
Mock Graph so tests never hit a live tenant.
Should assertions check behaviour.
slides.narration: A module you cannot test is a module you cannot safely change. Pester is the PowerShell testing framework. You describe a function, write It blocks for each behaviour, and use Should assertions to check the result. The killer feature is Mock, which lets you replace a Graph cmdlet with a fake that returns whatever you want, so your tests never touch a live tenant. Here we mock the managed device call to return nothing and assert our function throws. Now you can refactor with confidence.

slides.title: Recap & your task
bullets: Module = .psm1 code plus .psd1 manifest.
Export only public functions; hide helpers.
Throw meaningful errors; log and retry.
Protect behaviour with Pester tests.
Task: build the EndpointOps module with a test.
slides.narration: Let us recap. A module is a p s m one of code plus a p s d one manifest, generated with New dash Module Manifest. Export only your public functions and keep helpers like Write dash Log and Invoke dash With Retry internal. Throw meaningful error records, log through Write dash Verbose, and wrap flaky calls in retry with backoff. And protect it all with Pester. Your task: turn at least two earlier functions into a module called Endpoint Ops, generate the manifest, export only the public functions, wrap a Graph call in Invoke dash With Retry, add Write dash Log, and write one Pester test that mocks the Graph cmdlet and asserts a throw when no device is found. See you in lesson seven.
